title: Inside the computer: CPU and RAM
summary: What the processor, the memory and the disk each do, and why a program is loaded before it runs.

scheme: does the         holds what       keeps files,
text: Three parts do almost everything:
- the CPU (processor) does the work: it runs instructions;
- the RAM (memory) holds the programs and data in use right now;
- the disk keeps your files, even when the power is off.
The CPU can only run instructions that are in RAM (the disk is also far too slow). So a program is first copied from the disk into the RAM, then it runs.
- Power off, and the RAM is empty: whatever wasn't saved to disk is lost.
- That's why you save your work: saving means writing to the disk.
A CPU only does tiny steps: add two numbers, compare them, copy a value, jump to another instruction.
- It repeats that loop billions of times per second. A 3 GHz clock ticks 3 billion times a second.
- Everything you see on screen is built from those tiny steps.

scheme: 120 other processes sleep or wait their turn
text: A core runs one thing at a time. A CPU today has several cores, so a few things really run at once.
- There are many more processes than cores: most of them sleep, waiting for you or a timer. The kernel switches the others very fast, so they all seem to run together.
- Many CPUs run 2 threads per core, so nproc can show twice the number of cores.
$ nproc          # how many threads the CPU runs at once

scheme: registers ▸ cache ▸ RAM ▸ SSD ▸ hard disk
text: The closer to the CPU, the faster and the smaller.
- The CPU keeps what it uses most close by: in registers, and in the cache, which fills itself automatically.
- When the RAM is full, Linux can move some of it to the disk (swap, if set up), and everything slows down.

scheme: total  used  free shared buff/cache available
text: free -h shows the RAM. Read the last column, available.
- Linux fills unused RAM with a cache of recent files: most of it is given back as soon as a program needs it.
- So a small free is normal. A small available means the RAM is really short.
$ lscpu | head      # your CPU
